extracted.intended_audience: Members of Parliament and the informed British public (contemporaneous readers concerned with India policy)
extracted.subtask_description: A parliamentary speech and pamphlet-style critique attacking ministerial handling of Company debts, corruption, and administration in India, arguing principles of justice, public finance, and procedural fairness. It targets government conduct, Company servants, and creditors (e.g., Benfield) in late-18th-century India affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles to avoid suspicion in settling pecuniary transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of plain principles the speaker says ought to be observed to avoid suspicion in settlements involving public money and contested debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact guidance given: 'First, to hear all parties equally, and not the managers for the suspected claimants only; not to proceed in the dark, but to act with as much publicity as possible; not to precipitate decision; to be religious in following the rules prescribed in the commission under which we act; and, lastly, and above all, not to be fond of straining constructions, to force a jurisdiction, and to draw to ourselves the management of a trust in its nature invidious and obnoxious to suspicion.' If these rules are observed, corruption ought not to be suspected; if violated, suspicion will attach in proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of tribute requires provision of protection/equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribute (payments/tributes levied) is legitimate only when accompanied by the sovereign's ability and duty to protect; tribute 'hangs on the sword.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker argues that imposing tribute without corresponding protection or equivalent is absurd and oppressive. Example: condemning Tanjore to pay a perpetual tribute to the Nabob of Arcot who has been deprived of military power and therefore cannot provide protection; such a charge is illegitimate and cruel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt fiscal burdens to the subject's ability; do not measure strength by imposed burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing charges or tributes, authorities must calculate the proportion of burden relative to the people's ability and leave funds sufficient for future reproduction of revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes ministers for taking no steps to 'furnish grounds for a just calculation and estimate of the proportion of the burden and the ability.' It condemns estimating 'the strength of the bearers by the burden they impose' and calls for care to leave funds sufficient for the reproduction of revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not condition means of subsistence (natural-resource rights) on political payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights to essential natural resources (e.g., river water for irrigation) must not be linked to political arrangements or used as instruments of extortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The use of the Cavery river was 'given to the Rajah, and a power provided for its enjoyment at his own charge,' while the means to furnish that charge were cut off — effectively making water-use a tool to enforce tribute. The speaker insists such essentials of subsistence should be 'immutable' and not made to depend on political conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating or perpetuating usurious and compound debts
rubrics_metrics.description: Public or quasi-public arrangements must not generate or sanction extortionate debts bearing ruinous rates of interest, especially compound interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speech denounces the debts imposed on Tanjore and others — described as generating 'an usury the most completely ruinous... forty-eight per cent, payable monthly, with compound interest.' It condemns practices that load a people with debts that can only be paid by 'new usuries.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not permit collusion or conflicts of interest between ministers and private creditors/agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers must not ally with or protect private creditors, agents, or contractors who have concealed or corrupt interests in public claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker adduces the Benfield/Atkinson example: ministers rewarding Benfield's agent with offices and tolerating Benfield's return despite prior renunciation of claims. He argues that when those in authority provide for a person's interest 'on the real, but concealed state of his affairs,' it must be presumed they are in confederacy with him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect lawful jurisdiction and established decision-makers; do not supersede without hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not usurp the decision of bodies vested by law (e.g., Court of Directors) or adjudicate without hearing the parties and the authorized decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The speaker criticizes the minister for superseding the Directors (in whom the law vested decision of a territorial dispute) and for never hearing the Directors or the parties. He holds that such procedures speak to the spirit of the decision and warrant suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accountability and precaution when using public revenues for private indemnification
rubrics_metrics.description: When public funds or national revenues are to be charged in favor of private claimants or creditors, the decision requires heightened scrutiny, publicity, and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text condemns charging 'upon an undone country, in favor of a handful of men' sums amounting to millions sterling and argues that ministers should not silently or precipitately authorize such burdens; doing so without inquiry facilitates oppression and corruption.
